title: Logging library — severity, throttling, aggregation, then production
label: multi
statement: Build a logging library in the four reported phases — severity filtering, tests, throttling identical logs within a window, aggregating what was suppressed — then make it survive production: many threads, slow or failing sinks, bounded memory.
provenance: Reported for LinkedIn's AI-enabled round by more than one source. Reported wording: "Design a Logging Library with Severity Filtering, Rate Limiting, and Aggregation" — four phases: (1) a logger initialised with a minimum severity (DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR) that prints only logs at or above it; (2) unit tests; (3) throttling: an identical log (same severity, function name, line number and message) repeated within a window prints once; (4) aggregation: when the window expires and the next identical log arrives, print a summary of the suppressed logs using the timestamp of the first occurrence in that window.

stages.title: Severity filtering
stages.say: Implement a logger that is initialised with a minimum severity — DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR — and prints a log only if its severity is at or above that minimum.
stages.require: Implement `Logger(min, clock, sinks)` and `Log(sev, func, line, msg)`. Write `"{now} {sev} {func}:{line} {msg}"` to every sink. A sink that throws must not stop the others.
testNames: a throwing sink does not stop the next

stages.title: Throttle identical logs
stages.say: The console is being spammed. If an identical log — same severity, function name, line number and message — repeats within a time window, print only the first occurrence and suppress the rest.
stages.require: Add `Logger(min, clock, windowMs, sinks)`. Within `windowMs` of the first occurrence, identical logs are suppressed. A different line number is not identical.
testNames: different line number is not identical

stages.title: Aggregate what was suppressed
stages.say: Instead of dropping duplicates silently: when the window expires and the next identical log comes in, print a summary of the suppressed logs, using the timestamp of the first occurrence in that window.
stages.require: On the first identical log after the window expires, write a summary line starting with `"{firstTs} {sev} {func}:{line} {msg}"` and containing `"suppressed {count}"`, then the new log. No summary if nothing was suppressed.
testNames: summary stamped with the first occurrence
no summary when nothing was suppressed

stages.title: The throttle table grows
stages.say: Messages contain request ids, so almost every message is distinct. What happens to your throttle table over a day?
stages.require: Add `int PurgeExpired()` that removes windows that have expired with nothing suppressed, and returns how many it removed.

stages.title: 10,000 threads
stages.say: 10,000 threads are logging at once and the sink is slow. How do you stop logging from becoming the bottleneck — and from overwhelming downstream?

prompts.label: Check my design — no code

flaw.ctx: You asked for a logger that never blocks callers and reports how much it dropped.
flaw.answer: Under `BoundedChannelFullMode.DropWrite`, **`TryWrite` returns true even when it drops the item**. The drop counter never moves. Measured: **accepted 10,000, dropped 0, written ~1,050**. The dashboard says nothing was lost while nine in ten logs were. (My own first AsyncLogger had this bug; the 10,000-thread test caught it.)
flaw.fix: `FullMode = Wait` with non-blocking `TryWrite` (returns false when full), or the `itemDropped` callback overload of `CreateBounded`.

qa.a: O(1) average for lookup, insert, remove; O(n) worst case if many keys collide. Enumeration is O(n) and order is not guaranteed.

Separate chaining, but without node objects: an `int[] buckets` of indices into an `Entry[]` array, each entry carrying its hash, key, value and a `next` index. Colliding keys form a chain through `next`.

When the entries array is full it grows to a larger prime (about double) and every entry is rehashed into new buckets — O(n) for that insert, amortised O(1). Pre-size with the constructor capacity when you know n.
Removing does not shrink anything: freed slots go on a free list for reuse. `TrimExcess()` shrinks. A struct key that is large is copied into every entry.

Only code that locks the *same object*. `lock (x)` is `Monitor.Enter/Exit` on x's object header, in a try/finally. It also acts as a full memory barrier, so writes inside are visible to the next locker.
Yes, with two locks taken in different orders (D5), or with a call out to unknown code while holding the lock. One lock and no callouts cannot deadlock. `Monitor` is re-entrant for the same thread.

Uncontended, a lock is tens of nanoseconds. Contended, threads spin briefly then block, causing context switches; throughput collapses toward one thread's worth. The fix is less work under the lock, or more locks (striping).
`this`, a `Type`, a string — other code can lock them too. Use a private readonly object (or `System.Threading.Lock` in .NET 9+).

qa.q: What does a bounded Channel do when full?
qa.a: Depends on `FullMode`. `Wait`: `WriteAsync` waits, `TryWrite` returns false. `DropWrite/DropNewest/DropOldest`: drops and `TryWrite` returns **true** (R14).

qa.q: When Interlocked instead of a lock?
qa.a: A single-word update with no invariant tying it to other fields — counters. Two fields that must agree need a lock.
SemaphoreSlim can be awaited (`WaitAsync`) and counts beyond 1; it is not re-entrant and must be released in a `finally`.

qa.q: Does async create a new thread?
qa.a: No. `async` lets a method be suspended; `await` on an incomplete task returns to the caller and schedules the rest as a continuation. No thread exists for the waiting.

The OS completes the I/O (I/O completion ports on Windows, epoll on Linux) and the continuation is queued to the thread pool or the captured context. The thread was free the whole time — that is the point.

Cooperatively. You pass a `CancellationToken` down; APIs that accept it observe it and throw `OperationCanceledException`. Nothing is aborted from outside. Blocked primitives need a registration to wake them (BoundedBlockingQueue does this).

qa.q: Can you await inside a lock?
qa.a: No — the compiler forbids it, because the continuation may run on another thread. Use `SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync` with `Release` in a `finally` (R12 is what happens without the finally).

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: Build a logging library in the four reported phases — severity filtering, tests, throttling identical logs within a window, aggregating what was suppressed — then make it survive production: many threads, slow or failing sinks, bounded memory.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- `Log(severity, function, line, message)`; levels DEBUG < INFO < WARN < ERROR; print only ≥ the configured minimum
- Identical = same severity, function, line and message; within the window, print the first only
- When the window has expired and the next identical log arrives, print a summary: count suppressed, stamped with the first occurrence
- Multiple sinks; one failing sink must not affect the others or the caller
- Thread-safe; logging must never become the request path's bottleneck

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Two different problems hide in one class. **Deciding** what to print is small, shared state (the throttle table) — guard it with a short lock. **Writing** is slow I/O — never do it under that lock, and in production never do it on the caller's thread at all: enqueue into a bounded buffer and let one background writer drain it. When the buffer is full you drop and count, because a logger that blocks requests has turned an observability tool into an outage.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: Phases 1–4: `Logger` with an injected `IClock`, a `Dictionary<Key, Window>` (key = severity, function, line, message) under one lock, sinks written outside the lock. Production: `AsyncLogger` over `Channel.CreateBounded` with `FullMode = Wait` and non-blocking `TryWrite`, one pump task, per-sink try/catch, Interlocked metrics, and a bounded `DisposeAsync` that drains.

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- Filter by severity before anything else — no lock for discarded logs.
- Under the lock: look up the key. Inside the window → count it, return. Expired → capture a summary if anything was suppressed, reset the window. New → open a window.
- Outside the lock: write the summary (if any), then the line, to every sink, each in its own try/catch.
- Async: TryWrite into the bounded channel; false → increment dropped. The pump drains with `ReadAllAsync`.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Type | Why |
|---|---|
| enum Severity | Ordered values make filtering one comparison |
| readonly record struct Key | Value equality and hashing for "identical" for free |
| Dictionary<Key, Window> | The throttle table: window start, first timestamp, suppressed count |
| IClock | Window tests without sleeping |
| Channel<string> (bounded) | Back-pressure and a single reader, without writing a queue by hand |
| Interlocked counters | Metrics read by a scraper without taking a lock |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
- Filter by severity before anything else — no lock for discarded logs.
- Under the lock: look up the key. Inside the window → count it, return. Expired → capture a summary if anything was suppressed, reset the window. New → open a window.
- Outside the lock: write the summary (if any), then the line, to every sink, each in its own try/catch.
- Async: TryWrite into the bounded channel; false → increment dropped. The pump drains with `ReadAllAsync`.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md: Log is O(1) expected: one dictionary lookup under a short lock, plus the writes. AsyncLogger.Log is O(1) and never waits. Memory: O(distinct live keys) for throttling, O(capacity) for the buffer.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
- DEBUG under an INFO minimum is filtered.
- Three identical WARNs within 1 s → one line.
- Same message on a different line number is not identical.
- After the window, the next identical log prints a summary stamped with the first occurrence ("suppressed 2"), then itself.
- No summary when nothing was suppressed.
- PurgeExpired removes 1,000 one-off windows — the throttle table is bounded.
- A throwing sink does not stop the next sink.
- **10,000 concurrent callers** (32-way): accepted + dropped = 10,000 exactly, and written = accepted (2,291 / 7,709 at capacity 1,024 in one run).
- A sink that always throws: 5 failures counted, the pump keeps running.

learn.title: 10 · Tests
learn.md:
**S1 — Severity filtering**

- below the minimum is filtered
- at or above is written
- format
- the minimum itself passes
- every sink receives it
- a throwing sink does not stop the next

**S2 — Throttle identical logs**

- duplicates within the window suppressed
- different line number is not identical
- different severity is not identical

**S3 — Aggregate what was suppressed**

- summary + the new line
- summary stamped with the first occurrence
- summary carries the count

**S5 — 10,000 threads**

- the sink saw exactly what was written

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- Delegate the enum, the record key and the sink interface — pure boilerplate.
- Own the throttle state machine (new / inside window / expired-with-suppressed) — write it yourself or specify it exactly.
- Ask for tests with the Tests template, and check every expected timestamp in the summaries.
- If the assistant proposes `BoundedChannelFullMode.DropWrite` with a drop counter, ask what `TryWrite` returns when it drops — then check the docs.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe filtering by an ordered enum before any locking, a short lock around a Dictionary of throttle windows keyed by (severity, function, line, message), and writing to the sinks outside that lock. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call Log, from many threads concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."
- *Complexity check* — "What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it."
- *Requirement change* — "The requirement changed: Add Logger(min, clock, windowMs, sinks). Within windowMs of the first occurrence, identical logs are suppressed. A different line number is not identical. List which members need to change and which do not, before writing any code."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Writing to the sink inside the lock (R11).
- `DropWrite` with a counter on `TryWrite == false` — under DropWrite, TryWrite returns **true** when it drops, so drops are silent (R14). **My own first version did exactly this**; the 10,000-thread test reported 10,000 accepted, 0 dropped, 1,026 written.
- An unbounded throttle table keyed on messages that contain request ids.
- `DateTime.Now` in the throttle — tests then depend on wall-clock timing.
- Summary stamped with the expiry time instead of the first occurrence (the reported spec says first occurrence).

**Verification exercise:** Incorrect API assumption — Under `BoundedChannelFullMode.DropWrite`, **`TryWrite` returns true even when it drops the item**. The drop counter never moves. Measured: **accepted 10,000, dropped 0, written ~1,050**. The dashboard says nothing was lost while nine in ten logs were. (My own first AsyncLogger had this bug; the 10,000-thread test caught it.)

learn.title: 13 · Concurrency considerations
learn.md:
Shared state: the throttle table (and, async, the channel). Two threads logging the same key at once must not both print it: the read-decide-update of the window is one critical section. Writing to sinks is deliberately outside it — the review exercise R11 holds the lock across I/O and serialised 200 calls into ~460 ms.

**Level 3 — Concurrency**

- *10,000 threads logging simultaneously — what is shared?* — Throttle table → short lock; the sink → off-thread
- *Lock or ConcurrentDictionary for the throttle table?* — Read-decide-update per key: one lock (or AddOrUpdate with care)
- *Could synchronisation become the bottleneck?* — Only if I/O is inside it; otherwise stripe the table by key hash

learn.title: 14 · Scalability considerations
learn.md:
**Level 4 — Scale**

- *Logs overwhelm downstream.* — Bounded buffer, drop-and-count, sampling, batching
- *Millions of distinct messages.* — Purge expired windows; cap the table

learn.title: 15 · Production considerations
learn.md:
- Metrics: accepted, dropped, written, sink failures, buffer depth. **Alert on drops** — that is data loss in your observability.
- Configuration: minimum level and window per logger, changeable at runtime without a restart.
- Shutdown: complete the channel, drain with a deadline, report what was lost.
- Never log secrets; redact at the call site or in a sink filter.

**Level 5 — Productionisation**

- *What do you alert on?* — Drops and sink failures
- *The log sink is down for ten minutes.* — Buffer then drop with counts; fallback sink
- *Deploying a config change to the level.* — Runtime-reloadable, no restart

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
- *Severity filtering.* — Ordered enum, one comparison, before any locking.
- *Unit tests.* — Inject the clock and a recording sink; test window edges exactly.
- *Throttle identical logs.* — Key = (severity, function, line, message) as a record struct; window per key.
- *Aggregate the suppressed.* — Summary on the first identical log after expiry, stamped with the first occurrence.
- *10,000 threads logging at once.* — The throttle lock is held for a lookup only; writes happen outside it. Beyond that: per-thread buffers or the async logger.
- *Logging must not become the bottleneck.* — Callers enqueue into a bounded channel and return; one background writer does the I/O.
- *Do not overwhelm downstream.* — Bounded buffer + drop-and-count; per-key throttling; sampling of DEBUG; batching writes to the sink.
- *A sink fails.* — Per-sink try/catch, a failure counter, and a fallback (stderr) — never an exception into the caller.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *Null or empty message? Unknown severity? Window of 0?* — Validate or log as-is — decide; window 0 disables throttling

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Cost per Log call?* — O(1) expected; filter before the lock
- *Where is the bottleneck?* — Sink I/O — it must not be under the lock

aiGuide.intro: The freshest reported AI-round question (5 reports, Aug–Sep 2026). Four phases, then production. Lesson 11.2 of the video course runs this exact question.
plan: Ask: what makes two logs identical? is the minimum itself written? can I inject the clock?
AI fills in Log → read its assumptions → run

Threads: decide under the lock, write outside it; AI writes the stress test

stages.name: Severity filtering
stages.yours: Write the class shape: minimum severity, an injected `IClock`, an array of sinks. One comment per rule: the exact format `"{now} {sev} {func}:{line} {msg}"`, and that a failing sink must not stop the others. Three tests, including **the minimum itself is written**.
bad: Write a logger in C# with severity filtering.
A new static `Logger` with its own `LogLevel` enum, `DateTime.Now` and `Console.WriteLine`. Your tests do not compile.
A different library: no sinks, no clock, not your class
Console output: nothing to assert on
good:
C#. Implement Log in the Logger class below. Drop any log below _min. Write "{now} {sev} {func}:{line} {msg}" (now = _clock.NowMs) to every sink. A sink that throws must not stop the others. Keep my fields and signatures; add no public members. List your assumptions before the code. Show only Log and any private helper.
<Logger.cs pasted>
stages.reply: Typical defect: assumption 2 says "a log **at exactly _min** is dropped too", and the code has **`sev <= _min`**. You find it in one sentence before reading the code.
validate: A log at exactly the minimum is written
A throwing sink does not stop the next one
stages.say: "The assistant read *below* as *at or below* — its assumption said so. One character, so I fixed it myself."
stages.require: Implement `Logger(min, clock, sinks)` and `Log(sev, func, line, msg)`. Write `"{now} {sev} {func}:{line} {msg}"` to every sink. A sink that throws must not stop the others.
stages.say_iv: Implement a logger that is initialised with a minimum severity — DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR — and prints a log only if its severity is at or above that minimum.

stages.name: Throttle and summarise
stages.yours: Add a key record (severity, function, line, message), a window (start, suppressed count), a `Dictionary` of windows and **one lock that guards only that table**. Say the rule: **decide under the lock, write outside it**. Tests: three identical logs, then one after the window — the summary carries the **first** timestamp.
stages.ai: **Co-generate** the new Log, against your table and lock.
bad: Add rate limiting so duplicate logs don't spam.
Keyed by the message only, `DateTime.UtcNow`, writes to sinks inside its lock, and no count or summary.
"Duplicate" undefined: a Warn and an Error with the same text collide
Half the requirement (the summary) is missing
good: Add throttling to Log using the _windows table and _gate I added. Identical = equal LogKey. Inside windowMs of a window's start: count it, write nothing. After the window: if any were suppressed, first write "{firstTs} {sev} {func}:{line} {msg} [suppressed N]", then the line, and start a new window. Decide under _gate; call the sinks outside it. Show only Log. Keep my fields. No DateTime — use _clock. State your assumptions about the window boundary first.
stages.reply: Typical defect: the summary stamped with **now** instead of the window's first timestamp. The boundary and the lock are usually right.
validate: Exactly at start + window: a new window, the log prints
Different line number or severity: not identical
Window expired with nothing suppressed: no summary line
Sink calls are outside the lock
Windows for one-off messages must be purged — say how
stages.fix: A narrow follow-up: **"The summary must use the window's first timestamp, w.Start, not now. Change only that line."** Never "that's wrong, fix it".
stages.say: "Decide under the lock, write outside it — a slow sink must never serialise every caller."
stages.require: On the first identical log after the window expires, write a summary line starting with `"{firstTs} {sev} {func}:{line} {msg}"` and containing `"suppressed {count}"`, then the new log. No summary if nothing was suppressed.
stages.say_iv: Instead of dropping duplicates silently: when the window expires and the next identical log comes in, print a summary of the suppressed logs, using the timestamp of the first occurrence in that window.

stages.name: Production: never block the caller
stages.yours: Requirement first: **Log never blocks**. Design: a **bounded** channel, **one** background writer (keeps order), **drop and count** when full, drain on dispose. Then write one check yourself: three numbers must add up — accepted + dropped = calls, written = accepted.
stages.ai: **Co-generate** the AsyncLogger. The design is in the prompt; the Channel API is boilerplate.
bad: Make logging async so it doesn't block.
No bound: a burst of a million logs is a million queued tasks
No order: tasks run in any order
No way to flush at shutdown
A failing sink → an exception nobody sees
good: Write AsyncLogger: Log(severity, message) must never block. Put lines in a bounded Channel<string> of the given capacity; one background task writes them to the sinks. If the channel is full, drop the line and count it. Expose Metrics (Accepted, Dropped, Written). DisposeAsync stops accepting and drains. Keep my Logger unchanged; no Task.Run per call. Explain what Log does when the channel is full. Show only AsyncLogger.
stages.reply: Typical defect (measured): **`FullMode = DropWrite`** with drops counted when TryWrite returns false — but under DropWrite, **TryWrite returns true even when it drops**. "Accepted 10,000, dropped 0, written 1,024." Reading does not find this; your three-numbers test does.
validate: Memory is bounded by the capacity
accepted + dropped = calls; written = accepted after dispose
Log only calls TryWrite — never the waiting WriteAsync
A throwing sink is counted, and the writer keeps going
stages.fix: Follow-up: **"Under DropWrite, TryWrite returns true even when it drops, so Dropped stays 0. Use FullMode.Wait — TryWrite never waits and returns false when full — and keep counting on false. Change only the options."**
stages.say: "Drop-write hides drops. With Wait plus TryWrite, the counter is honest and the caller still never blocks."
stages.require: Add `AsyncLogger(Severity min, int capacity, params ILogSink[] sinks)` implementing `IAsyncDisposable`: `bool Log(sev, msg)` never blocks; a bounded buffer drops (and counts) when full; one background writer drains to the sinks; `Metrics` returns `(long Accepted, long Dropped, long Written, long SinkFailures)`; `DisposeAsync` drains what was accepted.
stages.say_iv: 10,000 threads are logging at once and the sink is slow. How do you stop logging from becoming the bottleneck — and from overwhelming downstream?
